metadata.title: AI software is sinking, why is Accenture winning $84.5B deals?

content.text:
Investing.com and Yahoo Finance LLC may earn commission or revenue on some items through the links below.
Investing.com — High-flying enterprise AI software names have spent the past month getting crushed as corporate CFOs scrutinize software seat licenses. Palantir (NASDAQ:PLTR) tumbled 17.8%, Snowflake (NYSE:SNOW) slid 16.5%, and CrowdStrike (NASDAQ:CRWD) dropped 12.0% over the past 30 days. Yet Accenture (NYSE:ACN), the IT consulting and systems-integration giant, surged 17.0% over the same stretch to $249.95.
Wall Street still prices Accenture like a legacy consultancy that AI will automate out of work, but its latest results show AI adding to its order book. Fortune 500 enterprises have realized that standalone AI software licenses deliver little without cleaned-up legacy data and retrained workflows—work that demands large-scale, human-led systems integration. Accenture captures that consulting bottleneck without bearing chip capex or software obsolescence risk, yet even after the rally its shares still trade well below InvestingPro's Fair Value estimate.
Identifying when a valuation discount reflects slower growth rather than a mispricing is what ProPicks AI is created for. In Tech Titans, InvestingPro's strategy dedicated to high-margin tech leaders, Accenture is passed over in favor of higher-growth technology names—including an enterprise IT infrastructure turnaround, a specialized semiconductor foundry, and a dominant chip-inspection equipment leader.
See the higher-growth tech names Tech Titans holds instead: Explore the Tech Titans strategy on InvestingPro
The Integrator AI Cannot Skip
Accenture's moat comes from sitting between AI software and the enterprises that have to make it work. It brings the scale that work demands: about 814,000 employees across more than 120 countries, including nearly 110,000 AI and data professionals.
Fiscal 2026 results proved that AI is adding work rather than taking it away. Fourth-quarter revenue grew 7% in local currency to $18.7 billion, beating estimates by $650 million, while adjusted EPS of $3.29 topped consensus by $0.10. More than 400 new clients started advanced AI work during the year, emerging AI and data partner bookings more than tripled, and full-year bookings reached $84.5 billion for a 1.1 book-to-bill ratio.
That demand converts into heavy cash generation. Full-year revenue rose 5% in local currency to $74.2 billion, adjusted EPS climbed 8% to $13.97, and free cash flow reached $11.6 billion. Accenture returned a record $11.5 billion to shareholders in fiscal 2026, up 38% year-over-year, and plans to return at least $9.5 billion in fiscal 2027—including a 5% dividend increase and $5.5 billion in share repurchases.
Fair Value Outruns a Street Stuck at Hold
Wall Street has not followed the rebound. Most recent ratings are Holds—Wells Fargo and Baird at $252 and TD Cowen at $201—while UBS rates the shares a Buy at $275 and Goldman Sachs a Buy at $260. The average analyst target of $229.74 now sits below the share price.
InvestingPro's Fair Value models place intrinsic value at $340.84 per share, about $111 above the Street's average target. The stock trades at 18.7 times trailing earnings and pays a 2.58% dividend yield.
The main risk is that growth slows faster than AI demand builds. Fiscal 2027 guidance calls for 3% to 6% local currency revenue growth, but only about 3% is organic, with acquisitions supplying 2% to 2.5%. Management flagged lower pricing in many areas of the business in the fourth quarter, the Middle East remains an approximately $1 billion annualized revenue headwind, and 14 analysts cut EPS estimates over the past 90 days.
Before buying into a 17% consulting rebound, investors must weigh Accenture's AI bookings momentum against slowing organic growth. Generative AI bookings conversion rates, federal government contract exposure, and operating margin guidance are detailed inside the Accenture Pro Research Report.
Evaluate AI bookings conversion, federal contract exposure, and operating margin guidance: Access the Accenture Pro Research Report on InvestingPro
From AI Bookings to Organic Growth
Software buyers can cut seat licenses, but they cannot skip the integration work that makes AI run inside their own systems. Accenture has shown that work is growing, and the next test is whether organic growth reaccelerates enough to win over a Street that still rates it a Hold.
Relying on a single consulting giant while enterprise IT budgets switch between software vendors and integrators leaves capital exposed to slowing organic growth. Rather than attempting to guess which consulting or software balance sheet will win the next IT budget cycle, InvestingPro's data-driven strategies evaluate thousands of balance sheets every month to isolate companies turning enterprise AI demand into verified free cash flow.
